provenance.rightsNote: Lectio Edition (SDIT): clear modern English of Dante, synthesized from the public-domain translation tradition (Longfellow 1867; Cary 1814; Norton's prose 1892) and checked against the Italian; modern verse translations consulted, not quoted. Verse lines kept. In progress, canto by canto.
sourcesCited: Charles Eliot Norton, prose (1892, public domain)
modern verse translations (Ciardi, Mandelbaum, Hollander, consulted, not quoted)

character: Plain modern English — the sense of the original, made to read with ease today.
overview: The Lectio Edition renders Dante in clear modern English that keeps the forward pull of the journey and the sharpness of his images, without the inversions and archaism of the older verse. Kept line by line, canticle by canticle.
introduction: Longfellow's 1867 Dante is faithful and grave, but its nineteenth-century inversions slow a modern reader. The Lectio Edition keeps Dante's line-by-line structure and his concrete, startling imagery — the dark wood, the gates of Hell, the souls like autumn leaves — in English that moves the way Dante moves. The older verse translations and the Italian are a tap away.

divergences.older: a forest dark (Longfellow); a gloomy wood (Cary)
divergences.note: Longfellow's inverted 'a forest dark' is the kind of nineteenth-century word-order that trips a modern reader; the Italian is plainly noun-then-adjective, 'dark wood.' We keep it concrete and unadorned — it is the canto's master image.

divergences.lectio: the place where the sun is silent
divergences.note: Dante writes that the sun is silent, not merely dark — a deliberate crossing of senses (a place where light has gone so dead it has no voice). We keep the strangeness rather than tidy it into 'where the sun never shines.'

The veltro's (Greyhound's) birthplace is one of the most debated lines in the poem — whether 'feltro' means the towns Feltre and Montefeltro, humble felt cloth, or something else. The line is meant to be a riddle, so we keep it as a riddle rather than resolve it for the reader.

divergences.phrase: Beatrice am I, who do bid thee go
divergences.older: I am Beatrice, who do bid thee go; / I come from there, where I would fain return; / Love moved me, which compelleth me to speak.
divergences.lectio: I am Beatrice, who send you on this. / I come from the place I long to return to. / Love moved me, and makes me speak.
divergences.note: Italian 'Amor mi mosse, che mi fa parlare' — the engine of the whole rescue is love, stated plainly. We keep the simple subject 'Love' so it lands as a force, not a flourish, and drop 'fain'/'compelleth.'

divergences.phrase: I not Aeneas am, I am not Paul
divergences.older: I not Aeneas am, I am not Paul, / Nor I, nor others, think me worthy of it.
divergences.lectio: I am not Aeneas, I am not Paul. / Neither I nor anyone thinks me worthy of it.
divergences.note: Dante's 'Io non Enea, io non Paulo sono' is two stark, parallel denials — the hinge of the canto's self-doubt. We straighten Longfellow's inverted word order so the repetition hits like the original's, with nothing between the reader and the names.

divergences.older: all contained / Within the heaven that has the lesser circles
divergences.lectio: all that the smallest of the heavens holds
divergences.note: 'Il ciel c'ha minor li cerchi sui' is the sphere of the Moon, whose orbit is smallest — i.e., everything beneath the heavens, the whole sublunary world. We name the cosmology plainly rather than reproduce Longfellow's 'lesser circles,' which leaves a modern reader guessing.

divergences.older: All hope abandon, ye who enter in! (Longfellow); All hope abandon, ye who enter here (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Abandon every hope, you who enter here.
divergences.note: The most famous line carved over Hell's gate. Longfellow's inverted 'All hope abandon, ye who enter in' is exactly the archaic word-order The Vernacular removes. The Italian is a plain, terrible imperative — verb, object, then the address — so we keep it that way: 'Abandon every hope.' We say 'every' (ogne) rather than 'all,' since Dante stresses each separate hope being given up, and 'here' for the gate the reader is standing at.

divergences.phrase: che fece per viltade il gran rifiuto
divergences.older: Who made through cowardice the great refusal (Longfellow); who in his cowardice / Made the great refusal (Cary)
divergences.lectio: who out of cowardice made the great refusal
divergences.note: Dante deliberately leaves this shade unnamed — most readers take it for Pope Celestine V, who abdicated the papacy, but the poem will not say so. We keep the figure anonymous and keep the resonant phrase 'the great refusal' intact rather than explaining it, because the withholding is the point.

divergences.phrase: Come d'autunno si levan le foglie
divergences.older: As in the autumn-time the leaves fall off (Longfellow); As fall off the light autumnal leaves (Cary)
divergences.lectio: The way the leaves let go in autumn
divergences.note: The canto's central image — the dead dropping one by one into Charon's boat like falling leaves. Dante's verb is 'si levan' (lift away / let go), gentler and stranger than 'fall off.' We keep that releasing motion ('let go') so the simile carries the eerie willingness Dante gives it, matching the falling-leaves image already named in this edition's overview.

segments.text:
Midway along the journey of our life
I came to myself in a dark wood,
for the straight road had been lost.

How hard it is to say what it was like —
that wood, so wild and rough and unrelenting
the fear comes back the moment I think of it.

It was so bitter that death is hardly worse.
But to tell of the good I found there too,
I'll speak of the other things I saw.

How I came to enter it I can't say clearly,
so heavy was I with sleep at the moment
I wandered off from the true way.

But once I had reached the foot of a hill,
there where the valley came to an end
that had pierced my heart with dread,

I looked up and saw its shoulders
already wrapped in that planet's rays
that lead us straight down every road.

Then the fear grew a little quieter
that had lasted through the lake of my heart
all that night I'd spent in such misery.

And like a man who, gasping for breath,
drags himself out of the sea onto the shore
and turns to stare back at the dangerous water,

so my mind, still racing in flight,
turned back to look again at that pass
no living person has ever left.

After I had rested my worn-out body
I took up the climb again on the empty slope,
my lower foot always the steady one.

And there, almost where the climb began,
a leopard — quick and very light on its feet,
its coat all covered in spots —

would not move out of my path.
It blocked my way so completely
that again and again I turned to go back.

It was the early hour of morning,
and the sun was climbing with the same stars
that rode beside it when Divine Love

first set those beautiful things in motion.
So the hour of the day and the sweet season
gave me good reason to hope

even against that beast with its bright pelt —
but not enough to keep me from fear
when a lion came into view.

It looked like it was coming straight at me,
head high, in a fury of hunger,
until the very air seemed afraid of it.

And a she-wolf, who in her gauntness
seemed loaded down with every craving
and has made so many live in grief —

she laid such a weight on me,
such terror came off the sight of her,
that I gave up all hope of the height.

And like a man who gladly piles up gains,
but when the time comes that he loses them
weeps and despairs in all his thoughts,

that restless beast did the same to me:
coming on, pushing me back step by step
toward the place where the sun is silent.

While I was sliding down toward the low ground,
before my eyes someone appeared
who seemed faint, hoarse from long silence.

When I saw him there in the vast waste,
"Have pity on me," I cried out to him,
"whatever you are — a shade, or a real man."

He answered: "Not a man. I was one once.
My parents both came from Lombardy,
Mantuans, both of them, by birth.

I was born under Julius, though late in his day,
and lived at Rome under the good Augustus,
in the time of the false and lying gods.

I was a poet, and I sang of that just
son of Anchises who came out of Troy
after proud Ilion was burned to the ground.

But you — why turn back to all that misery?
Why not climb the mountain of delight,
the source and cause of every joy?"

"Then are you that Virgil, that fountain
that pours out so wide a river of speech?"
I answered him, my head bowed in shame.

"You, the honor and the light of all the other poets —
let the long study and the great love
that drove me to your book stand for me now.

You are my master, you are my author.
You alone are the one from whom I took
the noble style that has earned me my name.

Look at the beast that turned me back.
Save me from her, famous sage,
for she sets my veins and pulses shaking."

"You have to go another way,"
he answered, when he saw me weeping,
"if you want to escape this wild place,

because this beast that makes you cry out
lets no one pass along her road,
but harries him until she kills him.

Her nature is so cruel, so vicious,
that she never fills her greedy appetite —
after feeding she's hungrier than before.

Many are the animals she mates with,
and more there'll be, until the Greyhound comes
who will hunt her down to a painful death.

He won't feed on land or money,
but on wisdom, on love and courage,
and his birthplace will lie between felt and felt.

Through every city he'll drive her down,
until he's chased her back into Hell,
out of which envy first turned her loose.

And so, for your own good, I judge it best
that you follow me. I'll be your guide,
and lead you out of here through an eternal place,

where you'll hear the cries of the hopeless,
where you'll see the ancient spirits in their grief,
each one screaming for a second death.

And then you'll see those who are content
within the fire, because they hope to come,
whenever it may be, among the blessed.

because that Emperor who reigns above —
since I rebelled against his law —
wills that none come through me into his city.

He governs everywhere, but he rules from there.
There is his city and his high throne.
Happy the one he chooses for it!"

And I said to him: "Poet, I beg you,
by that same God you never knew,
so that I escape this evil and worse,

lead me to the place you spoke of,
so I may see the gate of Saint Peter
and those you call so wretched."
Then he set out, and I followed behind.

The day was leaving, and the darkening air
was letting the creatures of the earth
rest from their labors; I alone

was making myself ready for the struggle —
the hard road and the suffering both —
which memory, which does not fail, will trace again.

O Muses, O high genius, help me now.
O memory, that wrote down what I saw,
here your true worth will show.

I began: "Poet, you who guide me,
look at my courage — is it enough,
before you trust me to this brutal pass?

But if the enemy of all evil
was gracious to him, thinking of the great effect
that would come of it — who he was, and what —

and that empire, if we want the truth,
was founded as the holy place
where the heir of greatest Peter sits.

On this journey you give him such credit for,
he heard the things that were the cause
both of his victory and of the papal robe.

Later the Chosen Vessel went there too,
to bring back proof for that Faith
which is the first step on salvation's road.

But I — why would I go? Who grants it?
I am not Aeneas, I am not Paul.
Neither I nor anyone thinks me worthy of it.

So if I give myself up to this coming,
I'm afraid the coming may be folly.
You are wise; you understand better than I can say."

And like a man who unwills what he willed,
and on second thought changes his intention
so that he backs out of it completely,

that's what I became on that dark slope:
by thinking I burned up the whole undertaking
that had been so quick to start.

"If I have understood your words rightly,"
answered that shade of the great soul,
"your spirit is touched with cowardice,

which often weighs a man down so
it turns him back from a worthy enterprise,
the way a trick of the eye spooks a shying beast.

To free you from this fear,
I'll tell you why I came, and what I heard
the first moment I felt pity for you.

I was among those who hang in suspense
when a lady called to me, so fair, so holy
that I begged her to command me.

Her eyes shone brighter than the stars,
and she began, gentle and low,
in an angel's voice, in her own tongue:

'O courteous spirit of Mantua,
whose fame still lasts in the world
and will last as long as the world goes on,

a friend of mine — not a friend of fortune —
is blocked on the empty hillside
so badly that he has turned back in terror,

and may already be so lost, I fear,
that I have risen too late to help him,
from what I've heard of him in Heaven.

Go now, and with your polished speech
and whatever else he needs to get free,
help him, so that I am consoled.

I am Beatrice, who send you on this.
I come from the place I long to return to.
Love moved me, and makes me speak.

When I stand again before my Lord,
I'll praise you to him often.'
Then she fell silent, and I began:

'O lady of virtue, you alone
through whom the human race rises above
all that the smallest of the heavens holds,

your command pleases me so much
that to obey, even if already done, would feel late.
You need say nothing more of what you want.

But tell me why you don't shrink
from coming down here into this center
from the wide place you burn to go back to.'

'Since you so deeply want to understand,
I'll tell you briefly,' she answered me,
'why I'm not afraid to enter here.

The only things one ought to fear
are those that have the power to harm.
The rest, no — they are nothing to dread.

God in his mercy made me such
that your misery does not touch me,
nor any flame of this burning reach me.

A gentle lady is in Heaven who grieves
at this hard place I'm sending you to,
so that strict judgment up above is bent.

She called Lucia and made her plea:
'Your faithful one is in need of you now,
and I commend him to your care.'

Lucia, the enemy of all that's cruel,
rose and came to where I sat
with ancient Rachel at my side.

'Beatrice,' she said, 'true praise of God,
why don't you help the man who loved you so
that for you he left the common crowd?

Don't you hear how pitiful his weeping is?
Don't you see the death that fights him
beside a flood the sea itself can't boast of?'

No one in the world ever moved so fast
to seize their good or flee their harm
as I did, after those words were spoken.

I came down here from my blessed seat,
trusting in your honest, dignified speech,
which honors you and all who've listened to it.'

After she had spoken to me this way,
weeping, she turned her shining eyes aside,
and that made me all the quicker to come.

And so I came to you, as she wished.
I took you out of the path of that wild beast
that blocked the short climb up the lovely mountain.

So what is it? Why, why do you hold back?
Why let such cowardice nest in your heart?
Why don't you have the daring and the nerve,

when three such blessed ladies
are caring for you in the court of Heaven,
and my own words promise you so much good?"

Like little flowers, bent down and shut
by the night's chill, that lift themselves
all open on their stems once the sun whitens them,

that's what I became, with my worn-out strength,
and so much courage poured into my heart
that I began, like a man set free of fear:

"O she of such compassion, who came to my aid,
and you, so gracious, who obeyed at once
the words of truth she gave you —

Go now — one single will moves both of us.
You are my leader, my lord, my master."
So I told him; and when he started off,
I entered on the deep and savage way.

"Through me you go to the city of grief.
Through me you go to everlasting pain.
Through me you go among the people who are lost.

Justice moved my maker on high.
Divine power made me,
the highest wisdom, and the first love.

Before me nothing was created
but things eternal, and I last forever.
Abandon every hope, you who enter here."

These words, in a dark color, I saw
carved over the top of a gate.
I said: "Master, their meaning is hard for me."

And he, like one who already knew, replied:
"Here you must let go of every doubt.
Every cowardice must die here.

We have come to the place I told you of,
where you will see the suffering people
who have lost the good of the mind."

And then he laid his hand on mine,
with a calm, glad look that steadied me,
and led me in among the hidden things.

There sighs and weeping and loud wailing
rang through the starless air,
so that at first I wept to hear it.

Strange tongues, monstrous accents,
words of pain, voices of fury,
high cries and hoarse ones, and the smack of hands —

all of it made a tumult that wheels on
forever through that air forever black,
the way sand swirls up when the whirlwind blows.

And I, my head ringed round with horror,
said: "Master, what is this I'm hearing?
Who are these people so broken by their pain?"

And he to me: "This wretched way of being
belongs to the dreary souls of those
who lived with no disgrace and no praise.

They are mixed in with that worthless choir
of angels who were neither rebels
nor faithful to God, but only for themselves.

Heaven cast them out, to keep its beauty pure,
and the depths of Hell won't take them either,
since the damned would find some glory next to them."

And I: "Master, what weighs on them so hard
that it makes them cry out like this?"
He answered: "I'll tell you, and keep it short.

These have no hope of ever dying,
and their blind life is so debased
they envy every other fate there is.

The world allows no memory of them.
Mercy and justice both look down on them.
Let's not talk about them — look, and move on."

And I, looking again, saw a banner
that ran in circles, spinning so fast
it seemed to scorn the thought of ever stopping.

And behind it came so long a line
of people, I would never have believed
that death had undone so many.

When I had recognized a few of them,
I looked, and I saw the shade of the one
who out of cowardice made the great refusal.

At once I understood, and I was sure,
that this was the crowd of worthless souls
hateful to God and to his enemies alike.

These wretches, who were never truly alive,
were naked, and were stung again and again
by the wasps and hornets swarming there.

The stings streaked their faces with blood
that ran down, mixed with their tears,
and was gathered at their feet by loathsome worms.

And when I turned to look still farther on,
I saw people along the bank of a great river,
and I said: "Master, tell me now,

so I may know who these are, and what law
makes them seem so eager to cross over,
as far as I can tell in this dim light."

And he to me: "All this will be made clear
to you, the moment we stop and stand
on the dismal shore of Acheron."

Then, with my eyes lowered in shame,
afraid my words had begun to annoy him,
I held my tongue until we reached the river.

And look — coming toward us in a boat,
an old man, white with the hair of age,
shouting: "Misery on you, you ruined souls!

Give up all hope of ever seeing the sky.
I come to carry you to the other shore,
into the eternal dark, the heat and frost.

And you over there — you, the living soul —
get away from these, for they are dead."
But when he saw that I would not go,

he said: "By another way, another port
you'll reach the shore to cross, not here.
A lighter craft will have to carry you."

And my guide: "Charon, don't fight it.
This is willed where what is willed is done,
so ask no more."

At that, the shaggy cheeks went still
on the ferryman of the livid swamp,
who had wheels of flame around his eyes.

But those souls, worn out and naked,
went pale and ground their teeth together
the moment they heard the cruel words.

They cursed God and cursed their parents,
the whole human race, the place, the time,
the seed they sprang from, the day they were born.

Then all of them drew back together,
weeping bitterly, toward the cursed shore
that waits for every man who does not fear God.

Charon the demon, with eyes like burning coals,
signals to them and herds them all aboard,
beating with his oar any soul that lags.

The way the leaves let go in autumn,
one after another, until the branch
sees all its riches lying on the ground —

just so the evil seed of Adam
throw themselves down from that bank one by one,
at his signal, like a bird answering its call.

So they go off across the dark water,
and before they have landed on the far side,
a fresh crowd is already gathering on this one.

"My son," the gentle master said to me,
"all those who die under the wrath of God
come together here from every land.

And they are eager to cross the river,
because the justice of Heaven drives them on
until their fear is turned into desire.

No good soul ever passes this way.
So if Charon complains about you,
you can understand now what his words mean."

When he had finished, the whole dark plain
shook so violently that even now
the memory of that terror bathes me in sweat.

The land of tears let out a blast of wind
that flared with a flash of crimson light,
and it overcame every sense in me,
and I fell, like a man taken by sleep.
